claims.text: The initial tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy has a largely supersaturated, single-phase BCC matrix.
A controlled heat treatment can induce stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitation in a tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy.
Heat treatment between 800°C and 1100°C with a stepwise temperature profile will produce the desired nanoscale precipitates.
The intervention produces coherent nanoscale δ and γ″ precipitates.
The coherent nanoprecipitates are uniformly distributed within a BCC matrix.
Coherent precipitate/matrix interfaces act as efficient sinks for irradiation-induced point defects.
The coherent interfaces enhance local recombination of irradiation-induced defects.
Enhanced defect recombination reduces the accumulation and growth of defect clusters.
Maintaining precipitate coherence facilitates dislocation transmission and avoids compromising ductility.
SCCPs can provide ultrahigh strength without sacrificing tensile ductility in a tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy.
The SCCP-treated alloy will exhibit lower irradiation-induced defect-cluster density and void swelling than the untreated baseline.
After fusion-relevant irradiation, the SCCP-treated alloy will maintain or improve yield strength and ductility relative to the untreated baseline.
The beneficial irradiation response will be pronounced at fusion-relevant irradiation and operating temperatures.
Outside the optimized thermal-processing window, precipitates may over-coarsen.
Precipitate over-coarsening may reduce defect-sink efficiency or adversely affect ductility.
Heavy-ion irradiation at elevated temperature adequately simulates the relevant fusion-reactor conditions for testing this hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome allows mechanical properties to be maintained or improved, but the falsification rule treats properties equal to the baseline as falsifying. Equality is therefore simultaneously presented as an acceptable and a falsifying result.
